paragraphs: Swamiji noticed one idea running through nearly every scripture and mythology: human beings today have slipped down from a higher state they once enjoyed. The Jewish scriptures express it as Adam's fall. Hindu texts speak of a golden Age of Truth, when no one died unless they chose to, when people could keep their bodies as long as they wished, and when minds were pure and strong, with no evil and no suffering. Our present age, in this view, is a decline from that perfection.

Alongside this idea, Swamiji pointed out, almost every culture tells of a great flood. The Old Testament has one, and so did the ancient Babylonians, Egyptians, Chinese and Hindus. The world kept getting worse until a flood swept much of humanity away, and then the slow climb back towards purity began again. The Hindu version goes like this.

Manu, a great sage of ancient times, was praying on the bank of the Ganga when a tiny minnow swam up to him, asking for protection from a bigger fish that was chasing it. Manu kindly dropped it into a pot of water he had with him and took it home. By the next morning, the little fish had grown to fill the pot and told Manu it could not stay there any longer.

So Manu moved it into a tank. The next day it was as big as the tank. He shifted it to a river, and by morning the fish filled the whole river. Finally Manu released it into the ocean. Then the fish revealed who it really was: the Creator of the universe, who had taken this form to warn Manu that a flood was coming to drown the world.

The fish told Manu to build an ark and bring aboard a pair of every kind of animal, along with his family. A horn would rise out of the water; Manu was to tie the ark to it. When the waters went down, he should step out and fill the earth with people again.

The flood came, and Manu saved his family, two of every animal and the seeds of every plant. When the water receded, he went out and repopulated the world. And that, the story says, is why we are called 'man': we are the descendants of Manu.
learn: The same stories turn up across very different cultures, which says something about how much humanity shares. Manu's simple kindness to a tiny fish ended up saving the world, so never treat a small good deed as unimportant.
